questions.problem: The point $P$ with coordinates $(3,6)$ lies on the curve $y=f(x).$ Which of the following points must lie on $y=\frac{1}{3}f(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The function $y=\frac{1}{3}f(x)$ represents a compression of the function $y=f(x)$ by a factor of $3$ parallel to the $y$-axis. This has the effect of dividing the $y$-coordinates of all points on $y=f(x)$ by $3.$

Therefore, the point $(3,6)$ on $f(x)$ is mapped to the point $(3,\frac{6}{3})=(3,2),$ and this point must lie on the graph of $y=\frac{1}{3}f(x).$

questions.problem: The point $P$ with coordinates $(3,-3)$ lies on the curve $y=3f(x).$ Which of the following points must lie on $y=f(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The function $y=3f(x)$ represents a stretch of the function $y=f(x)$ by a factor of $3$ parallel to the $y$-axis. This has the effect of multiplying the $y$-coordinates of all points on $y=f(x)$ by $3.$

The point $Q(3,q)$ on $f(x)$ is mapped to the point $P(3,-3)$ on $y=3f(x).$ Since we know that the $y$-coordinate of $P$ is $3$ times the $y$-coordinate of $Q,$ we can form the following equation:

$$
3q=-3
$$

Solving this equation, we get $q=-1.$ Therefore, the coordinates of $Q$ are $(3,-1).$

canonical_examples.problem: The point $P$ with coordinates $(-2, 2)$ lies on the curve $y=f(x).$ Find a point that must lie on the graph of $y= 7f(x).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function $y = 7f(x)$ represents a stretch of the function $y = f(x)$ by a factor of $7$ parallel to the $y$-axis. This has the effect of multiplying the $y$-coordinates of all points on $y=f(x)$ by $7.$

Therefore, the point $(-2,2)$ on $f(x)$ is mapped to the point $\left(-2, 7 \cdot 2\right) = (-2 , 14),$ and this point must lie on the graph of $y = 7f(x).$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
When we multiply a function by a constant, the graph either stretches out or compresses. Transforming a function in this way is called **scaling**.

To illustrate, consider the graph of $y=f(x)$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14218586/assets/21f9b06e470ca0e94605eb72c5a12d2a1f2ec56645588a960f12be81ad8252ec.png)

The following table lists four sets of points. The set of points in the left-hand column correspond to the graph of $y=f(x),$ and the set on the right-hand side corresponds to $y=2f(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Points on [math]y=f(x)[/math]} & \text{Points on [math]y=2f(x)[/math]} \\ (1,2) & (1,4) \\ (4,-3) & (4,-6) \\ (0,2) & (0,4) &  \\ (-2,0) & (-2,0)\end{aligned}
$$

For each point on the graph of $y=f(x),$ there is a point on the graph of $y=2f(x)$ with the same $x$-value and *double* the $y$-value. 

Now that we have four points on the graph of $y=2f(x),$ let's plot the full graph.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14218586/assets/262b6515b995f6fdcf7b959dc62d9599b71476471fbc2bde394dcebfd47cabc0.png)

We say that the graph of $y=2f(x)$ is the graph of $y=f(x)$ **vertically stretched** by a **scale factor** of $2.$ 

We can also say that the graph of $y=2f(x)$ is the graph of $y=f(x)$ stretched by a factor of $2$ **parallel to the $\mathbf y$-axis.**
